THE IDEA

A federal court ordered a West Virginia veterinarian to pay $956,709 in August 2025 after she could not account for 9,796 dosage units of oxycodone. In 2026 the per-record recordkeeping fine starts at $16,205 and caps at $19,246. A retired DEA supervisory special agent told dvm360 in the January-February 2026 issue that vets are now on every DEA investigator's annual work plan. An AAHA course led by that same ex-agent teaches that roughly 96% of vet practices will fail a DEA inspection on recordkeeping. And the practice manager at a Florida animal hospital says a normal reconciliation used to eat 40 minutes of searching PIMS codes, hunting lost papers, and living with 'did we / didn't we' moments before she found a real discrepancy.

This service reconciles the controlled-drug logs for independent vet clinics every month and hands back a closed audit file. A trained human (a CVPM, retired DEA diversion investigator, or veterinary compliance consultant) reviews the week's logs on top of whatever the clinic already uses (paper, PIMS, VetSnap, LogRx), chases every discrepancy, fixes missing signatures, tracks the biennial inventory clock, and signs a monthly packet the owner can hand a DEA agent at the door. Priced $499 to $1,499 per site per month by DVM count, with a $750 Compliance Snapshot as the frontend and a $2,000 to $5,000 multi-site retainer for practice groups. Not another dashboard. A completed deliverable.

WHY NOW

DEA put vets on every investigator's annual work plan

A retired DEA Supervisory Special Agent told dvm360 in the January-February 2026 issue that veterinarians are now part of the work plan for every DEA investigator, and audits are happening more often than ever. The investigator fiscal year starts October 1, so the 2026 wave is landing right now. The same agent runs a compliance consultancy and teaches the AAHA course. His message is one word: reconcile.

The math got worse in 2026. Under 21 USC 842(c)(1)(A), a single recordkeeping violation now starts at $16,205, adjusted for inflation. Owner Exchange, citing the Federal Register, puts the recordkeeping cap at $19,246 per violation and prohibited-act violations at $82,950 each. Every unaccounted-for dosage unit counts as its own violation. In August 2025, a West Virginia vet was ordered to pay $956,709, the maximum allowed, after investigators found 6,593+ dosage units of hydrocodone and oxycodone unaccounted for at her practice. In November 2024, a Cheyenne vet paid $30,000 after a tip triggered an inspection that turned up systemic recordkeeping gaps. Neither case was about diversion by the vet. Both were about paperwork the vet could not produce.

Practices with fewer than 10 employees made up 50.5% of all US veterinary establishments in 2022 (AVMA 2025 Economic State of the Veterinary Profession). That is roughly 17,000 small independents, the exact ICP for a done-for-you compliance service.

AVMA 2025 ECONOMIC STATE REPORT

A DEA study found that 37% of inspected veterinary clinics had discrepancies in their controlled substance inventories (cited by Cubex, DEA regulations guide, 2026). Discrepancies are the exact work this service resolves.

CUBEX (CITING DEA STUDY)

Veterinary Growth Partners cites a predicted average of 11 violations per practice with a fine up to $15,691 per violation on DEA inspection. At those numbers, one inspection can cost a small clinic over $170,000, dwarfing any subscription price.

Should you build this?

REASONS TO BUILD

The pain is real and priced: a WV vet paid $956,709 in 2025 after 9,796 unaccounted oxycodone units, and the 2026 per-record fine floor is $16,205. Owners will pay $500-$1,500/mo to make that risk go away.
The gap is clean. VetSnap and LogRx flag problems and hand them back. SafetyVet does one $4,450 on-site visit a year. Nobody sells a monthly closed audit file, which is exactly what an owner wants when a state investigator can walk in unannounced.
Timing has a federal signal you can point at: a retired DEA supervisory special agent told dvm360 in Jan-Feb 2026 that vets are on every investigator's FY2026 work plan. That is a talk-track you can use at every state VMA CE session this year.
Money math works for a solo boutique: 50 clinics at a $749 blended price is $449K ARR, and the honest ceiling on 17,000 small independents at 5-8% share is $8M-$15M. That is a great one- or two-person business, not a venture story.

Nobody Googles for this. Category search runs 90/mo and service-shaped queries return zero volume in Google Ads. The first 100 customers come from CE talks and CVPM forums, one clinic at a time, and that is a 9-12 month grind.
A retired DEA agent or CVPM has to sign the monthly packet. If the founder is a pure operator or coder, they hire that person in month two, which raises the capital number and caps how fast the service scales.
VetSnap owns the branded search (3,600/mo), the case studies, and the pricing page. If they add a $199/mo managed-reconciliation tier or partner with Titan Group, the wedge shrinks to paper clinics and mixed-PIMS practices only.
Awareness lags reality. Most independent clinics still treat DEA as a 3-to-8-year problem, so every sale starts with educating a scared but skeptical owner before you can quote a monthly price.
